data.title: Federal appeals court again denies Trump admin request to block 20,000 California ballots
data.description:
9th Circuit again denies Trump administration request to block 20,000 California ballots

Kevin Rector, Brittny Mejia
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 7:16 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A federal appeals court for the second time Friday denied a Trump administration request to block 20,000 ballots from California voters the administration alleges may be noncitizens — ruling that the administration had failed to show that "such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law."

The three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — ruled 2-1 that the U.S. Constitution gives the state and Congress the power to decide how elections are run, and that allowing the Trump administration to "misuse" federal statutes to "prescribe" how California must process ballots would "override the plain and manifest dictates of the Constitution itself."

"Because Congress has not exercised the specific power granted to it under the Elections Clause to override California's established laws for challenging ballots or removing ineligible voters, the State Legislature's statutory scheme remains the only method to do so," the judges found.

Advertisement

The panel's majority — comprised of Trump appointee Mark J. Bennett and Biden appointee Gabriel P. Sanchez — wrote that "if the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts."

They also wrote that separate federal law prescribes sweeping changes to voter lists 90 days prior to an election, especially given questions about the reliability of the Trump administration's list of purported noncitizens.

"The suspect reliability of these lists found by the district court reflects the concern Congress sought to mitigate with the 90-day quiet period," they wrote.

Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, the other Trump appointee on the panel, dissented — arguing that his colleagues erred in denying a basic request by the Trump administration to ensure only citizens are voting.

"The federal government proposes a modest remedy — stopping California from mixing the ballots of citizens and suspected noncitizens," Bumatay wrote. "This solution would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens. The district court, and now our court, denies this reasonable request."

This article will be updated.

data.title: Renewed Iran war after midterms could threaten fragile U.S. gains in Hormuz
data.description:
A resumed Iran war after midterms would put fragile gains in Hormuz to the test

Susannah George, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 2:16 PM UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The United States is pointing to gains in the Strait of Hormuz, intent on demonstrating that weeks of complex and secretive military operations there have returned oil flows to near prewar levels and chipped away at a key piece of Iranian leverage ahead of a threatened return to all-out war after the U.S. midterm elections next week.

An increase in vessel traffic and the small percentage of ships disabled by Iranian strikes are signals "clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway," read a statement this week from U.S. Central Command announcing that Brad Cooper, the head of the command, had visited the strait.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

But while U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf have welcomed the operations along with oil industry and shipping firms, serious questions remain about how sustainable they are in the face of escalating Iranian attacks, according to two people with knowledge of the matter and two Western officials based in the region, who like others interviewed for this report spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive information. Also unclear, they said, is whether the U.S. military would be able to maintain the operations in the strait at the same time as resumed heavy strikes on Iranian territory after the U.S. midterm elections, as President Donald Trump has threatened.

In addition to increasing the volume of strikes on shipping, Tehran also appears to have adjusted its targeting in recent weeks, increasingly taking aim at engine rooms to disable vessels rather than just damage them, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter, who is close to the shipping industry. United Nations data shows that two ships have sunk this month as a result of Iranian attacks.

The U.S. operations that have enabled the dramatic increase in oil exports are some of the most complex of the war, according to a European security official and the two people with knowledge of the matter. U.S. forces have integrated air defenses, fighter jets, drones and warships to protect vessels in layers as they pass through the waterway, running a harrowing gantlet of Iranian attacks far beyond what ordinary seafarers sign up to face on the job. The European security official likened the operations to creating "a bubble" that moves along the strait as vessels make the transit.

Iranian attacks have made this month the most violent in the waterway since the war began. At least 25 ships in the strait have been hit in October, according to data collected by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, a maritime monitoring body affiliated with the British military.

But oil exports have also surged during the same period. Figures vary, but maritime analytics firm Kpler found that average daily oil exports reached 14 million barrels for the week ending on Oct. 18, about 80 percent of prewar averages. The rebound has been remarkable: In July, daily averages over a seven-day period were as low as 7 million barrels. U.S. Central Command doesn't release daily averages, but it said that "since summer," oil exports through the strait had reached 1.5 billion barrels.

The U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division leads the mission and runs a joint operations center in the United Arab Emirates, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter.

The UAE Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the country's role in the Hormuz operations.

At least 30 ships per day have transited the strait so far this month, according to the two individuals with knowledge of the matter. U.S. Central Command has released little information publicly about efforts to protect shipping in the strait, but it said Sunday that over the past six months, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the waterway.

Speaking about his visit to the strait in a social media video Friday, Cooper said he saw a resumption of shipping but no signs of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "When I flew over the strait, I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting, all types - cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas," he said. "I didn't see the IRGC out there at all."

The resumption of traffic through the strait - which nearly ceased amid the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran - has brought a critical lifeline for U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf as well as the shipping and energy industries. "Everyone wanted this," said the second person with knowledge of the matter, who is in contact with industry leaders and government officials. But that person cautioned that the private sector and U.S. allies in the region view the effort as an imperfect, temporary measure. The two Western officials based in the region said they have heard similar concerns about the operations in the strait.

Since U.S. operations ramped up in August, seven seafarers have been killed and 18 injured, according to United Nations data. The risk levels are currently so high that nearly all the vessels willing to make the trip are state owned and operated. Most private companies continue to refuse to use the strait even under U.S. protection, according to the individuals and officials.

"The situation is completely unsustainable," said one of the Western officials based in the region. While vessel traffic has increased for oil exports, the official said, few vessels carrying liquefied natural gas have taken the risk. "If one of those gets hit, it's not just an oil spill; it's an explosion," the official said.

The fact that Iran has escalated attacks on shipping is itself a demonstration of U.S. successes in the waterway, according to Gregory Brew, an energy and Iran analyst at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy firm.

"The U.S. has achieved something pretty considerable, overcoming Iran's closure of the strait earlier this year, but it's not enough," he said, referring to energy prices that have remained high despite increases to traffic.

Iran has demonstrated that it doesn't need to completely close the waterway to keep prices high, but the U.S. has found that even partially reopening the strait isn't moving energy markets the desired amount, according to Brew. "As long as it's contested, then Iran is achieving their objective," he said.

But Kevin Donegan, a retired vice admiral who served in Bahrain as the commander of the Navy's Fifth Fleet, said he sees the operations differently. Compared with the escort operations of the "tanker wars" in the 1980s, current U.S. operations have a smaller footprint and are more nimble, he said.

"During the tanker wars, ships were lining up and being escorted with lots of naval vessels, big convoys," he said. "We'd brute-force them through in groups. That's not what's happening now."

Donegan said he couldn't share further details of the operations, but he described them as "a piece of maritime superiority" that can be turned on and off and moved to where vessels are most vulnerable.

"Think of it as a moving sanctuary," he said.

Every day, the vessels registered to make the crossing assemble off the coast of the United Arab Emirates and are delivered guidelines to follow, including the instruction to turn off the Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders that broadcast the vessel's location with satellite and radio signals. The vessels are then given coordinates marking the safe passageway, with labeled checkpoints denoted by the NATO phonetic alphabet.

Once the vessels have exited the strait, they transfer their cargo to privately owned ships in the Gulf of Oman before traveling back to the Persian Gulf to load up again. Because so few vessels are willing to risk Iranian attacks, roughly the same group of vessels is making the trip back and forth from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.

"It's a de facto shadow fleet," said the Western official based in the region, using a term to describe vessels that attempt to evade sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil by switching off AIS and moving oil with ship-to-ship transfers.

Donegan, the retired vice admiral, said the operations also appear to be having a secondary function: They are beginning to build the framework of a future regional coalition to counter Iran. He cited support for the operations from the Emirati, Kuwaiti and Iraqi governments.

The Trump administration "has to continue to build this coalition of countries saying that what Iran's doing is not acceptable," he said.

"The way forward is to get the Iranians to a tipping point."

Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 12:14 PM PDT 1 min read

US stocks plunged in the final trading day of the month as earnings from Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) this week rekindled concerns about the amount of money Big Tech is spending on its AI ambitions.

The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) tumbled 3.3% as a tech-fueled sell-off intensified. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 1.2%, or over 600 points, while those on the S&P 500 (^GSPC) dropped 2.2%.

The Nasdaq is on track for its worst month since March 2025.

(^DJI )

^DJI ^GSPC ^IXIC

Stocks fell for the second day in a row after Amazon and Alphabet posted rare earnings misses, renewing concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amazon shares fell 2%, while Alphabet continued to erase market value after its stock suffered its worst day in over 20 years.

Intel (INTC) also suffered a brutal reaction to its earnings report, dropping 30% in premarket trading after the company's Q4 outlook came up short.

One bright spot in the market was ExxonMobil (XOM) and Chevron (CVX), whose stocks briefly touched record highs after the oil majors reported that their earnings were boosted as refining margins widened amid the war in the Middle East. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca (AZN) also reported an earnings beat before the opening bell.

While earnings remain in focus, oil prices rebounded higher, putting additional pressure on markets. Brent crude futures (BZ=F) rose to $113 per barrel, while WTI crude (CL=F) reached $104 per barrel.

Bitcoin (BTC-USD) prices tumbled more than 5% as crypto assets were rattled following a $6.3 billion hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, marking the largest heist of its kind in history.

LIVE 15 updates
  • 12 mins ago
    David Hollerith

    Binance hackers using 'never-seen-before' tactics to move stolen billions, investigators say

    Hackers behind Binance's estimated $6.3 billion hack are moving stolen funds across blockchains in ways some investigators have never seen before, raising questions about whether artificial intelligence is helping them cover their tracks.

    Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said Friday that investigators observed thousands of transactions in a short period, suggesting the attackers are using automation to obscure the movement of stolen funds.

    "Our investigators are observing never-seen-before laundering patterns with the stolen funds from the Binance exploit," Chainalysis said in a social media post.

    It's too early to know whether AI is involved. Automated cryptocurrency transactions are not new, and investigators have yet to establish whether AI played any role in the attack itself.

  • 1 hr ago
    Ines Ferré

    Stocks at session lows as tech takes a hit, Nasdaq on pace for worst day since June

    Stocks fell to session lows in afternoon trading as the technology (XLK) sector took a hit.

    The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) tumbled 3.3% headed for its worst day since June. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 (^GSPC) dropped 2.1%.

    Crypto assets continued to slide, with bitcoin (BTC-USD) prices tumbling after a $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, marking the largest heist of its kind in history.

  • Today at 5:20 PM UTC
    David Hollerith

    Rates need to be higher, 2 Fed members say. The question is how much.

    Two members of the Federal Reserve suggested Friday that interest rates need to move higher to push down inflation, Yahooo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:

    St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem said he thinks inflation is too high and broad-based, and that the Fed needs to act "soon," otherwise higher prices will persist.

    Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin also suggested that the central bank needs to raise rates further to bring down inflation in the face of strong demand. The question is by how much.

    The Fed voted in a split decision this week to hold rates steady even as inflation has moved higher. A day later, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up in September, solidifying expectations for an interest rate hike in December

    Read more:

  • Today at 4:43 PM UTC
    Jared Blikre

    SpaceX has lost more than $400 billion in market value in less than a month

    Analysts spent last week raising their SpaceX (SPCX) price targets. Investors spent it selling the stock.

    SpaceX stock fell about 5% Friday, extending a slide that has erased more than $400 billion in market value since its high on Oct. 6, when the company was worth more than $2.3 trillion. It's now worth less than $2 trillion.

    The slide has wiped out SpaceX's post-earnings jump. The stock rose about 8% on Oct. 21 after third quarter results beat Wall Street's forecasts and has since lost more than $250 billion in value.

    Then came the lockup. About 1.3 billion shares became free to sell on Oct. 22, and SpaceX held above $140 in the sessions that followed. On Friday, it broke below that level.

    A close below $135 would be SpaceX's lowest since Aug. 24, and the next floor below that is the summer low near $107. To turn things around, bulls first need to reclaim about $147, which would put SpaceX back above $2 trillion, and then its $150 first-day open.

    Read more.

  • Today at 4:15 PM UTC
    David Hollerith

    Burger King's chicken nuggets just got a Whopper-like makeover — fries are next

    The turnaround at Burger King in the US continues to sizzle, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports.

    Burger King's US comparable sales increased a stunning 8.4% in the third quarter, parent company Restaurant Brands International (QSR) said in its third quarter earnings release this week.

    "I think people still look at fast food as a treat, and they want to treat themselves once in a while, and when they want to treat themselves, they don't want to compromise. They don't want to say, 'Well, I'm going to go get the cheap meal. Or the least expensive product, or the lowest-quality product.' They want to feel like they are treating themselves and they're being treated well," Burger King US president Tom Curtis said on Sozzi Unleashed.

    Read More:

  • Today at 3:30 PM UTC
    Ines Ferré

    Binance CEO on $6.3 billion hack:'We are committed to covering all hacked losses'

    Binance co-CEO Richard Teng promised exchange users impacted by the record $6.3 billion hack on his exchange that they will be made whole.

    "We are committed to covering all hacked losses through our company funds. Your assets are safe," said Teng on social media on Friday.

    Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. While the initial investigation indicated the involvement of a compromised laptop, further digging revealed additional points of breach.

    "This was a complex attack," said Teng. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."

    Binance said about $3 billion in assets have been "frozen on-chain so far" with the help of partners like Tether and Circle. Customer withdrawals should resume by Sunday, Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a separate social media post.

    The Thursday attack has rattled crypto markets and related stocks. Bitcoin (BTC-USD) tumbled 5% to around $76,600.

  • Today at 2:13 PM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    Reddit, Pinterest, and Roblox stocks tank after Q3 earnings

    Three digital stocks founded in the aughts — Reddit (RDDT), Roblox (RBLX), and Pinterest (PINS) — are all suffering from post-earnings stock drops on Friday morning.

    Reddit stock fell 24%, Roblox is down 16%, and Pinterest has declined 6%,

    Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferré details what's behind each move:

    Reddit posted weaker-than-expected daily active users in the third quarter and issued a current-quarter revenue forecast that fell short of Wall Street estimates.

    Wall Street also assessed the discussion platform's plan to only allow access to forums to logged-in account holders. Reddit said it will start testing login requirements during the fourth quarter across select international markets before rolling out the change worldwide.

    Roblox's third quarter results beat loss and revenue expectations, but daily active users fell 9% year over year to 138 million.

    Meanwhile, Pinterest reported third quarter revenue of $1.17 billion versus $1.21 billion expected by Wall Street. Adjusted earnings of $0.46 also came in below anticipated estimates of $0.49. Record users did not translate into expected advertising revenue, while European regulatory changes pressured cross-border advertising.

    Read more.

  • Today at 1:38 PM UTC
    David Hollerith

    US stocks open Friday lower with tech earnings denting AI enthusiasm

    US stocks opened lower Friday as disappointing earnings from Amazon and Intel deepened a tech sell-off and renewed worries about massive spending on artificial intelligence by tech giants.

    The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) tumbled 2.5% as a tech-fueled sell-off showed no sign of letting up. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 0.3%, while those on the S&P 500 (^GSPC) dropped 1.3%.

    (^DJI )

    Go deeper with AlphaSpace
    51,631.08 -711.48 (-1.36%)
    As of 3:18:37 PM EDT. Market Open.
    ^DJI ^GSPC ^IXIC
  • Today at 1:18 PM UTC
    Brian Sozzi

    The 'Magnificent 7' stocks are seeing stunning declines

    Call it the Unflattering 7.

    Long known as the Magnificent 7 stocks, shares of Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Amazon (AMZN), Tesla (TSLA), Meta (META), and Google (GOOG) are acting anything but magnificent, especially compared to their 52-week highs.

    Meta and Alphabet are effectively in bear markets, down more than 20% from their 52-week highs, as the Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace graphic shows below. Tesla is off by 19.2%, Amazon by 15.1%, and AI chip darling Nvidia by 12.2%.

    Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, and Tesla have been crushed following their earnings reports that showed pressured free cash flow amid aggressive AI spending. Nvidia is down because of the fear that all of these hyperscalers are overspending and will be forced to pull back in 2027.

    Read more.

  • Today at 12:27 PM UTC
    David Hollerith

    Crypto stocks set to open lower after record-breaking crypto heist

    Bitcoin (BTC-USD) prices tumbled to around $77,000 on Thursday night, and crypto-related stocks are set to open lower on Friday after crypto exchange Binance confirmed what industry watchers have identified as the biggest crypto hack in history.

    "The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B," said Binance on X. "We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far."

    (BTC-USD )

    Go deeper with AlphaSpace
    76,270.25 -4,473.04 (-5.54%)
    As of 7:18:34 PM UTC. Market Open.

    Binance said it "will cover all losses" from its Secure Asset Fund for users and company reserves.

    Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers

    Shares of Circle (CRCL), trading platforms Coinbase (COIN) and Robinhood (HOOD), and digital-asset Treasury giant Strategy (MSTR) are each down more than 6% in Friday's premarket.

    Read more.

  • Today at 11:56 AM UTC
    Brian Sozzi

    Intel and Sandisk have very different views about what's going on in memory chips

    Intel (INTC) stock is getting torched in premarket trading on Friday, falling 26%, after the company warned of sluggish PC sales in the current quarter. At the core of that warning is consumer resistance to the higher PC prices stemming from the memory chip shortage.

    Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan sees more challenging quarters ahead due to memory chip dynamics.

    "Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability," Tan said. "Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets. The pace of this PC correction has accelerated over the last two months as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell-through."

    On the other hand, hop onto the earnings call late Thursday from memory chipmaker Sandisk (SNDK), and you would've heard that there is no memory chip shortage at all. Or, at the very least, things stand to improve nicely in the months ahead.

    "We think our internal models are every segment in the NAND market," Sandisk CEO David Goeckeler said. "PCs, smartphones, data center will all show positive growth next year because content per device continues to go up as part of that is mixing to premium."

    Read more.

    (INTC )

    Go deeper with AlphaSpace
    63.65 -28.42 (-30.87%)
    As of 3:18:37 PM EDT. Market Open.
    INTC SNDK
  • Today at 11:00 AM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record

    Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre writes:

    Wall Street spent the week punishing Big Tech's biggest AI spenders. Amazon (AMZN) just posted the deepest cash burn in its history.

    Amazon's free cash flow — the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses, and equipment — was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September, according to its third quarter results released Thursday. That's nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.

    One quarter did most of the damage. Amazon spent about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

    Read more.

  • Today at 10:00 AM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    Oil rises on signs US could renew strikes on Iran

    Bloomberg reports:

    Oil rose on signs the US may resume military strikes against Iran, risking fresh turbulence in the region that may hurt energy flows.

    West Texas Intermediate gained toward $103 a barrel, after swinging more than $3 in the previous session, while Brent settled near $115. A top commander briefed President Donald Trump on military options on Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported. The US leader has repeatedly given signals he may restart airstrikes against Tehran after midterm elections next week.

    In Iran, one of the country's top negotiators, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested the Islamic Republic's positions on ending the war will not be compromised. His remarks followed confirmation from Tehran that officials had received a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance.

    Global benchmark Brent has rallied by 12% in October, hitting a six-month high, as the conflict has dragged on. The gains this month have come despite a revival of flows from the Middle East, with producers managing to ship cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz even with elevated risks to shipping.

    Read more.

  • Today at 9:00 AM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    Yen gains after BOJ, AI jitters drive Treasury rally, weigh on dollar

    Reuters reports:

    The yen inched higher on Friday after the Bank of Japan held rates steady as expected, while the dollar tracked Treasury yields lower as a fresh wave of selling in AI shares triggered a flight ‌to safety.

    The BOJ left interest rates on hold at 1.25% in a widely anticipated move, but revised up its inflation forecast and ‌stressed anew its readiness to continue pushing up borrowing costs to forestall mounting inflation risks.

    Following the decision, the yen strengthened to a high of 157.115 per dollar, erasing most of ​its losses for the month and putting it on track to end October broadly flat.

    Read more.

  • Today at 8:00 AM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    Good morning. Here's what's happening today.

    Economic data: Employment cost index, third quarter (+0.8% expected, +0.9% prior); MNI Chicago PMI, October (54.6 expected, 58.8 prior)

    Earnings calendar: ExxonMobil (XOM), AbbVie (ABBV), Chevron (CVX), AstraZeneca (AZN), BP (BP), Sanofi (SNY), General Dynamics (GD)

    Catch up on some top stories you might have missed overnight:

    Sandisk delivers solid results and an 8-for-1 split

    Reddit to limit access for logged-out users in strategy shift

    Amazon stock slides after Q3 earnings miss

    BOJ keeps rates steady, declares victory in hitting price target

    Andy Jassy says Prime Video is on track to earn 'tens of billions of dollars'

data.title: ICE agent indicted on aggravated assault charge for allegedly hitting man with car
data.description:
An ICE officer has been charged after striking a man with a car in Houston

ANNA WILDER and LEKAN OYEKANMI
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 3:37 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

CORRECTION Immigration Enforcement Houston

1 of 2
Carmen, sister of Miguel Parra Hernandez, holds a sign during a news conference about the Immigration and Customs Enforcement action involving Hernandez, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Houston. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via AP) Correction corrects first name to Carmen. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via AP)

HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was charged Friday with aggravated assault, prosecutors said.

The Harris County District Attorney's office says Mario Alberto Morales was behind the wheel of an unmarked black vehicle on Oct. 10 when it struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away. Parra Hernandez was later placed in custody with a broken leg.

Few federal officers during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown have faced criminal charges for their actions in the field, although some encounters have come under investigation.

Advertisement

The case in Houston was brought by District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, who is also investigating the fatal shooting of a Mexican homebuilder in July that set off protests in the nation's fourth-largest city.

ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and called accusations that the officer intentionally struck him false and "reckless." It called the indictment harging Morales with second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon "a political stunt" and said local officials to not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," ICE said in a statement.

Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speeds over a median and drives toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone.

The video shows a steering wheel, with Morales making a few sharp turns, and at one point, it appears the car has shaken as it runs over something. Morales gets out of the car and turns around, where Parra Hernandez is on the ground. Parra Hernandez and Morales speak in Spanish for a few seconds as Parra Hernandez grabs his leg, yelling in pain.

Morales says, "He got hit with a car, bro," and, "I was coming in and I hit him with the car."

Morales was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare, who said prosecutors have been in touch with the officer's attorney. Teare would not provide information on where Morales lives or who his attorney is.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day and was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.

Teare's office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.

Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.

FIEL hopes that the indictment of Morales would help with their plea to have him released from custody, said Cesar Espinosa, the group's executive director.

Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation

Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence "either intentionally or through gross negligence." He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had "weaponized his vehicle" before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Teare has not given a timetable for when his office's investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.

___

Wilder reported from Austin.

___

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

data.title: Pentagon reportedly tells NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia
data.description:
Exclusive-Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say

By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 5:04 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas

Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.

Among the nations that have received ‌messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, ‌which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.

Advertisement

The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The ​latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations."

Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.

Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. ‌Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.

None of the people, ⁠who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.

EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA

The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.

Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play ⁠into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.

Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.

Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.

One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a ​Baltic ​official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians.

The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting ​that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.

It was ‌not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.

"We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."

In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.

The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.

MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE

One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, ‌while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down ​the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions.

Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could ​dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.

The Pentagon messages to NATO officials ​come at a fraught time for European security.

Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.

On Wednesday, German prosecutors ‌said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a ​building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg ​area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.

At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued ​economic isolation.

Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a ‌process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent.

US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, ​particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.

(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius ​Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell)

data.title: Pope Leo casts historic U.S. vote after years of requesting both parties' primary ballots
data.description:
Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election

NICOLE WINFIELD
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 12:59 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

APTOPIX Vatican Pope

1 of 2
Pope Leo XIV waves as he arrives for his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square at The Vatican, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia) (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.

Advertisement

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it added.

This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they're also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin's retirement.

Leo's vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude's, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

Clashes with Trump

Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants.

Earlier this year, Trump called Leo "weak" and captive to the "radical left."

Responding to Trump's public rebuke, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for."

"I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems," he said.

The public dispute has subsided in recent months.

___

AP editor Holly Meyer contributed from Nashville, Tenn.

data.title: 2 men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's ballot. Now the DOJ is issuing subpoenas.
data.description:
Politics

DOJ issues new subpoenas in Alaska Senate probe, asks judge to intervene over "conspiracy" involving 2 Dan Sullivans

By
Nicole Sganga
Homeland Security and Justice Correspondent
Nicole Sganga is CBS News' homeland security and justice correspondent. She is based in Washington, D.C., and reports for all shows and platforms.
Read Full Bio
Nicole Sganga

Updated on: October 29, 2026 / 7:52 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

The Justice Department has begun issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal investigation into Alaska's Senate race, including the alleged efforts by Democrats to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News.

The subpoenas are targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody involved in the race has been charged with a crime.

The department also amended its civil lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion," adding in details from a New York Times report on alleged efforts by people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from Sullivan. The new filing calls the situation a "conspiracy to undermine the integrity of the electoral process."

Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel S. Sullivan has said in the past he is genuinely interested in running.

During a briefing with reporters Thursday, a Justice Department official offered perspective into the department's investigative approach in its criminal probe, saying there had been a "significant increase in activity" surrounding the Alaska race over the previous 24 hours. The Times report was published on Wednesday.

The Times' article detailed internal emails and text messages from individuals with knowledge of the alleged recruitment efforts — information the official suggested might significantly expand the government's ability to pursue its criminal investigation, since such communications are historically difficult for investigators to obtain without search warrants or voluntary cooperation from individuals with access to the material.

The official also alluded to possible investigative steps, like preservation requests to technology companies, search warrants for electronic communications and grand jury subpoenas seeking documents or testimony from those allegedly involved.

Asked what federal crimes could be implicated by an alleged recruitment scheme, the Justice Department official identified two civil rights statutes, 18 U.S.C. Sections 241 and 242, as potential roads for prosecutorial action.

Section 241 prohibits conspiracies to interfere with federally protected rights, including voting rights, while section 242 centers on willful deprivation of rights under color of law. The official added that prosecutors might, in a situation like this, examine whether there was a coordinated effort to trick voters into selecting a candidate.

The official referenced the federal prosecution of Douglass Mackey, convicted of conspiracy for posting misleading messages online during the 2016 election falsely encouraging Hillary Clinton supporters to vote by text message. That conviction was ultimately overturned by a federal appeals court in 2025.

Still, a Justice Department official acknowledged that the agency was not aware of any confirmed instances in which an Alaska voter had mistakenly cast a ballot for the wrong Dan Sullivan.

"I think I've not heard of that, but it's hard to tell exactly," the official said when asked whether voters had reported confusion or attempted to correct their ballots.

Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed a separate state investigation this week, ordering Alaska's Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law and whether criminal or civil action is merited.

CBS News has reached out to the Department of Justice, Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment.

Separate civil lawsuit also expands

The criminal investigation is ramping up alongside a separate civil lawsuit filed by the Trump administration last week, seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election results under certain circumstances if the Republican incumbent loses.

That lawsuit addresses the government's concerns that votes intended for Sen. Sullivan could instead go to Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whose candidacy was previously challenged by state election officials but ultimately greenlit by Alaska's Supreme Court.

The suit, which argues Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include the Times' reporting. It now includes a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a "conspiracy."

"Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief. It also aligns with common sense," the amended complaint reads.

Alaska officials have previously asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that election administration is a state responsibility.

During Thursday's briefing, before the suit was amended, Justice Department officials largely characterized the civil lawsuit as an effort to preserve the government's ability to challenge an election result if deemed necessary.

"I don't see this as much more than a preservation suit," one official offered, arguing that once ballots are counted and separated from envelopes, establishing whether individual voters were confused becomes increasingly challenging. 

The official also expressed interest in obtaining discovery concerning what Peltola's campaign knew about the alleged recruitment operation, and furthermore, when campaign officials may have learned of it.

President Trump has railed against the Alaska ballot situation, calling for Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be taken off the ballot. Asked by reporters about the Justice Department's lawsuit, he said last week: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'Do it.'"

data.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies and opts for phone calls as Election Day nears
data.description:
2026 Election

Trump cancels weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas in favor of holding numerous tele-rallies

Senate races in both states are considered toss-ups and could be key in either party’s path to control of Congress.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Oct. 29, 2026, 11:19 PM EDT
By Raquel Coronell Uribe

President Donald Trump announced Thursday he is canceling his rallies in Kansas and Iowa this weekend, where he had been set to stump for GOP candidates in competitive races, opting instead to do tele-rallies.

The rallies were to have been part of his planned midterm blitz, in which he said he would travel to 35 places across the country to help raise turnout for Republican candidates.

Trump has repeatedly touted what he believes is the positive impact of his rallies on GOP candidates, going as far as to suggest that his presence in battleground states has boosted Republicans in the polls.

But his tune appeared to change Thursday after his cancellations. Trump said he didn’t “feel I have to go to Kansas,” adding that he thinks Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who’s locked in a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton, “is doing well.”

Concerns over high costs connected to the war in Iran have helped turn the race into a toss-up in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate for nearly a century.

Trump, who has campaigned at 25 rallies in the past month, has admitted that the blitz has not been “easy,” saying through a hoarse voice Monday that “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”

But he insisted Thursday that he felt “perfect” and lashed out at a reporter who pressed him about whether the rally cancellation in Kansas was tied to his health.

“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell,” Trump said to the journalist.

He canceled in Iowa hours after that interaction, after a White House official and a person familiar confirmed that Trump’s appearance was off.

The Republican National Committee said in a news release that the rallies were canceled with the goal of “maximizing opportunities for President Donald J. Trump to speak to voters across the country.”

GOP operatives in Iowa, where all congressional races this year except one are competitive, told NBC News that in-person rallies would have been helpful. Trump’s rally Saturday would have been in Dubuque, in the contested 2nd Congressional District.

“A tele-rally will be helpful in boosting turnout, but an in-person rally would have been really helpful,” an operative said.

Another operative said he “would love to have the president,” but he said, “Iowa’s in pretty good shape.”

Trump is aiming to hold “more than 20” tele-rallies by Election Day, two White House officials said Thursday.

He is still scheduled to hold an event in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. He will be campaigning for Republican Rep. Randy Fine and Sen. Ashley Moody, who are running in races rated solidly Republican by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

No events have been announced for Monday.
